en: *Samguk yusa*, Royal Calendar, First Year:
Former Han Emperor Xuan, Wǔfèng Jiazi (4th year), Silla.

The first king, Heok-geu-se (Hyeokgeose), was surnamed Park and born from an egg; he ascended the throne at the age of thirteen in a *gaja* year (*jiazi*) and ruled for sixty years. His royal name was Yeongeoe (Yeonggoe), and his kingdom was called Seoraba (Seorabeol); it was also called Seobal, or erroneously Sira, or Gyeongrim. It was only during the time of King Geomnol (Gomnol) that the name Gyeongrim was first established.
This was the fourth year of the *gwanmu* cycle, the *muchen* year.
Huanglong (Yellow Dragon) year, Ren-shen;
Yuan-dì’s Chūyuán (Initial Origin) year, Gui-you;
Wǔ-yǒngguāng (Five Eternal Brilliance) year, Wù-yin. Five.
The sixth year of Jiǎzhào (Jiǎwèi), New Silla; the first year of Jǐshēn, Goryeo. Construction of the Golden Wall began in the first year of Dōngmíng-wáng (Jiǎshēn).
He ascended the throne at nineteen years of age. His surname was Gāo and his name was Zhūméng (also written as Zōuméng); he was the son of Tánjūn.
It was the fourth year of Jiànsī (Jǐchōu) of Emperor Chéng.
The fourth year of Heping, Guiyi;
the fourth year of Yanshuo, Dingyou;
the fourth year of Hongjia, Xinchou.
In the Yongshi era, year Yisi (105 BCE), four new kingdoms were established: Silla, Goryeo, and Baekje.
The second ruler was King Yuri (also written as Luli or Liu; son of Dongmyeong). He ascended the throne in Renyin (102 BCE) and reigned for thirty-six years. His surname was Ha.

First was King Wönjo (son of Dongmyeong’s third son, Gwi), who ascended the throne in Gui (101 BCE) and held power for forty-five years. His capital was Wŏiryeokseong (also known as Hacheon); it is now Jiksan.
The fourth year of Yuan-yan, the year Yi-you (14 B.C.E.), was the second year of Emperor Ai;
the fourth year of Jian-ping, the year Yi-mao (3 B.C.E.), and the third year, Bing-chen, saw the capital moved to Hanshan, which is present-day Guangzhou;
the second year of Yuan-shou, the year Ji-we (1 B.C.E.), was the reign of Emperor Ping.
The second year of the seventh cycle, the *gensil* (Original Beginning) *sin-u* (Heavenly Stem: Metal, Earthly Branch:

Fowl), was the twenty-second year of King Namhae, son of King Cheocheong and Queen Eoyeong of the Park clan; his consort was Lady Ungde. He ascended the throne in *gap-ji* (Earthly Stem: Wood, Heavenly Branch: Rat). Twenty years later, this king’s reign is also called the period of King Seogang Nyuji.

The first year of the second cycle, the *munsil* (Waning Moon), *mu-chin* (Earthly Stem: Earth, Heavenly Branch: Dragon), he moved the capital to the inner city within the kingdom, also known as Bureong, the New Palace.
The founding of the state was in the Jisi year;

the fifth day of the month of Wengjia in the Xushen year was the third [reign] of the Great Tiger Spirit King named Wuxi (also written as Weiliu), of the Xie clan. He was the third son of King Luli. He ascended the throne on the Wuyin day and ruled for twenty-six years.
Earth-Bird, Gengchen (178 CE), Year Three, Third Month, Day of the Nüli (or Nüniche) *jiǎshén*.

The father was Nanjie; the mother was Yun, the Consort of the Emperor. She was the daughter of King Ci Yao of the Jin clan. On *jiǎshén*, she was established as ruler for thirty-three years. The Nüniche (or Nüshijin) era began on *guīwèi* (the second day). Later Han, Year of the Tiger. *Note: The asterisk indicates that "Nüni" is a variant reading for "Nüniche.
The term "Ni" refers to the title of the Queen Mother.*

The thirty-first [ruler], King Minjung (Mingzhong), reigned from Jianwu (Jianhu) Bǐyǒu (Bǐyǒu) to the first year of the reign of King Mubong (Mùběn). He was the fourth king of Silla, Goguryeo, Baekje, and Gallaek (alternatively Gaya; present-day Jinju).
His name was Yeop (Yìp), his surname was Je (Xiè), and he was the son of Daeho (Dàhǔ). He ascended the throne in Jiǎchén (Jiǎchén) and ruled for four years.
He was the fifth king, Mubong.
The elder brother of Minjung was named Ae (also written as Ŭu);
he ascended the throne on the wu-shen day and reigned for five years.
He was the sixth king of the state of Zu.

The one named Gung (Myeonggung) is also called King Daejo (Daetjowang). He ascended the throne in the *Gichu* year and ruled for ninety-three years. The *Book of the Later Han* states that when he was first born, he could see with his eyes open. Later, he abdicated in favor of his younger brother, Prince Daeje (Daejaewang). The second son, King Doldu (Dowang), received the mandate;
his second son, King Munjo (Munjowang), ascended the throne in the *Eui* year and ruled for forty-nine years.

King Suru (Surowang) was born from an egg in the third month of the *Inyeom* year; he ascended the throne that same month and ruled for one hundred and fifty-eight years. Because he was born from a golden egg, his clan name is Kim (Geumse). This is recorded in the *Kaehwangneok*.
The middle element is *wǔ* (丙), the branch is *chén* (辰);

the second, fourth, and fifth [stages] are the liberation through shedding (*tuōjiě*, also read as *tùjiě*), and the *nichi* (尼叱) of the present and past lineages. The father is King Hándápo (含達婆) of Xiàguó (夏國)—also known as King Huāxià (花夏). The mother is the daughter of the King of Jījùnǚ (積女) and the consort of King Ānzhōngfǔ (阿中府). On the day *dīngyǐ* (丁巳), he established the principle for twenty-three years before the king passed away. He was water-buried in the *mò* (末) [region], and his bones were enshrined in a shrine at Dōngyuè (東岳), now known as the Great King of Dōngyuè.
The Ming Emperor’s *Yǒngnián* (永年) era, the fifth year of *wǔwǔ* (戊午), the eighteenth chapter. The Emperor.
The fifth year of the *Jianchu* era, the *bingzi* year: Posa Niche, now surnamed Park, was born;

his father was King No-ri and his mother was Princess Chiyao, the daughter of King Yi-so. On the *gengchen* day, he ascended the throne and reigned for twelve years. The third king, Mul-lu-jwa (King Daulu), son of [the previous king], was born on the *dingchou* day;
he ascended the throne and reigned for fifty-five years.
Three chapters harmonized in the Jiashen year of the Yuanhe era; two harmonies in the Dinghai year;
seventeen [chapters] in the Jichou year of Emperor Yongyuan’s reign; and the reign of Emperor Shangdi.
Yuanxing (Yisi), Emperor An’s Yanping (Bingwu),
Yongchu (Dingwei)— the seventh [cycle], Dharmakṣema. Now.

One version states his clan was Jīwèi (祇味) and his surname Pǔ (朴); his father was Bōsuō (婆娑), and his mother was Lady Shìxiào (史肖). His consort was the daughter of King Mòdì (磨帝), Lady Lǐ (禮). One version also states she was Lady Àilǐ (愛禮) of the Jīn (金) clan. He ascended the throne in the *rénzǐ* year and reigned for twenty-three years. During this king’s reign, the kingdom of Yīnzhì (音質)—now Ānkāng—and the kingdom of Yāláng (押梁)—now Qūshān—were extinguished.
[The years] Yuánchū (元初) were *jiǎyīn* (甲寅), and the sixth year of Yǒngníng (永寧) was *gēngshēn* (庚申).
Jianguang Xinyou; Yanyang Renxu;
the fourth, Shundi Yongjian Bingyin;
the sixth, the seventh, the fugitive sage-nun Nichijin.

Father No-ri was the elder brother of King Ji-ma; some say he was the consort of Queen Ji-ma. Lady Il-jik was the daughter of King Geom-mun. Lady No-no-ri was the daughter of King Ji-ma. Mother I-gan-sung was the consort of King No-no-ri; some say she was the consort of King No-no-ri of the Park clan. She ascended the throne in the *gapsu* year and reigned for twenty years.
Fourth, King Gae-ru, son of King Yi-ru, ascended the throne in the *euchin* year and reigned for thirty-eight years.
[In the] *yangga* year, *renshen*, the fourth.
Yonghe (6) Bingzi; Han’an (2) Renwu;
Jiankang (1) Jia Shen (Chongdi).
Yǒngjiā (Yǒngjia) Bǐyǒu (Bǐyou):
Emperor Běncǐ (Benchu) Bǐxū (Bǐxu); the seventh time, the Great King’s name was Suì (Suì), the Ancestor King;
younger brother of the Queen Mother, established in Bǐxū (Bǐxu) and reigned for nineteen years; Huán Dì (Huan Di).
Jianhe Dinghai (the third year),
Shaping Gengyin (the first year),
and Yuanjia Xinmao (the second year).
In the eighth year of Yongxing, the *gengsi* year, Ādaraṇi was enthroned.
Now, in the third year of Yongshou, the *yiwu* year, the National Ancestor King reached the age of one hundred and nineteen; his two elder brothers were both assassinated by the new king.
In the ninth year of Yanxi, the *wuxiu* year, he [the new king] also [received envoys] from the kingdom of Wa (Japan) at Geling, the eighth [reign] of the New Great King.
Named Bogo (also written as Boju); established in the fourteenth year of Lili, the fifth year of King Xiaogu (also written as Sogu).
Gaoluzi; established in the fiftyth year of Lili, the Bingwu year.
Established in the Dingwei year of Yongkang. This is the East Ridge of the Great Maitreya Courtyard at Xiange. Emperor Ling.
Jianning Wushen (4), Xiping Renzi (6),
Guanghe Wumwu (6); the ninth was King Guoguo Chuan.

He was named Nanhu (or Yimujia); he established his rule for twenty years. The state was called Guochuan (also known as Guohuai). He was buried at the site of Zhongping. It was the *jiayi* year, the ninth year of the era.

He attacked Huinichi; today it is Hongnong. Furthermore, during the Yonghan era of Emperor Xian, the *jisi* year— [Note: The provided text contains a mix of historical names, dates, and place names related to the Later Han period.]
First year of Chuping, Gengwu (192);
four years of Xingping, Jiashu (197);
second year of Jian’an, Bingzi (206). The tenth was Naehae Niche; now, the tenth is King San-shang, the sixth being King Ku-su.
One version states: "Noble; must resemble the son of antiquity. Established in the *jiawu* year, he reigned for twenty years.
Second, King Dengwang Shoulu, son of [King] Mu, with Queen Xu as consort. Established in the *jimao* year, he reigned for fifty-five years.
Surname Kim. Cao Wei Emperor Wendi Huangchu *gengzi*. Seventh, Emperor Ming.
The sixth year of the *dingwei* cycle of the Dahe era, the eleventh month;
the eleventh month of the *guichou* year of the Qinglong era of King Dongchuan.
The seventh king, Sapan (also written as Sapa...), son of Choushou, was immediately deposed.
In the *Jingchu* era, the *ding-si* year (237 CE), the third King [of Goguryeo] was Jang;
in the *geng-shen* year of the *Zhengshi* era (240 CE), the twelfth, King Li understood Niche (alternatively transcribed as *zhàn*).

King Li was the uterine younger brother of King Zu-ben. On the *ding-mao* day, he ascended the throne; fifteen years later, he first established diplomatic relations with Goguryeo. This was the eighth, King Gul.
The mother’s younger brother of Xiao Gu established [the reign] in Jiayin;
fifty-two years later, in Jiaisi of the Jiaping era; twelve years later, in the second year of Zhongchuangwang Gaoguxianggong;
and two years later, in Jiashu of the Zhengyuan era.
Ganlu (Amṛta), Bingzi (Bingzi year), the fourth [month], the third *ma* category.
The father of the King was King Juedeng; the mother was the daughter of Shenfuqing Shinfu. It is said that the Lady Zhen was established as ruler on Jiyu (Jiyou year).
Thirty-two years later, during the Jinyuan era of King Jingliu, Gengchen (Gengchen year), the fourth [month], the thirteenth day, the fourteenth *wei*, the nun Zhounichi [arrived]. Now.

One source reads "Mi-jo" (味炤); another reads "Mi-so" (未祖), and yet another "Mi-sho" (未召). His surname was Kim (金). He first established [the lineage]. His father was Ku-do (仇道), and his mother was born of Ge-mun-wang (葛文王). One source reads "Seul-rye" (述禮) instead. His consort was Lady I-bi (伊非), the daughter of Ge-mun-wang; she was the consort of Ju-beon-wang (諸賁王), and her name was Gwang-myeong-nang (光明娘). He ascended the throne in Renwu (壬午) and ruled for twenty-two years.
During the Tai-shi (泰始) era of Emperor Hu (虎帝) of the Western Jin, in the year Yi-you (乙酉), he was the thirteenth [ruler].
The thirteenth was Si-ch'wăn-wang (西川王), named Yak-ro (藥盧), also known as Yo-u (若友). He ascended the throne in Kyǒng-im (庚寅) and ruled for twenty years.
Xianning Bawei (535), the fifth year; Dakang Gengzi (560), the eleventh year. The fourteenth [ruler] was King Nichi (also written as Se-ri) of the Ju-ri clan.

His father was Jubeon, and his mother was Lady Park, née Jaso. In the Jiachen year (584), he ascended the throne. He ruled for fifteen years. He repaired and fortified the Moon City (Wolseong). The ninth [ruler] was King Gamje.
Guerzi (also written as Ze-ti, erroneously; established in Bingwu [326], reigned for twelve years).
During the Yuankang era of Emperor Hui, the year Xinhai [351], he was the fourteenth [ruler].
Fengshangwang Zhi-ge (whose name was Xiangfu) was established in Renzi [362] and reigned for eight years.
The fifteenth king, King Lin-ni-chih (alternatively transcribed as Ki-li), was the second son of the former King Che-chieh-zhi-jen.
His mother was Lady Ar. He ascended the throne in the year Wu-wu and ruled for twenty years. The tenth king, King Chen-chi, was his son;
he ascended the throne in the year Wu-wu and ruled for six years. The fourth king was King Chü-chih-mi.
One source states: His father was Mu (麻), his mother Haoqiu (好仇). He ascended the throne in the *xinhai* year and reigned for fifty-five years.
In the *renxu* year of the Dà'ān era, he was the fifteenth ruler of Mìchuān (美川).
Another account names him Miàoráng (妙禳) with the clan name Yǐfú (乙弗), also written as Yòufú (瀀弗). He ascended the throne in the *gēngshēn* year and reigned for thirty-one years.
Yonghegong (Eternal Prosperity) was the second son of King Chou of the second generation of the Bi-liu lineage,
the younger brother of Shapan; he ascended the throne in the Jiazi year and ruled for forty years.

In the years of Guangxi Bingyin and Dingmao, the national name was proclaimed as Silla. "Silla" means that virtue and achievement are renewed daily (*sin*), and it signifies the netting together (*na*) of the people of the four quarters.
Some say this dates from the era of Jijeung and Beopheung; others say it was during the Dingmao year of Emperor Huai’s Yongjia reign, the sixteenth year.

Gige Aeni Chikjeumjinseobyeo Yujo Angan (later known as King Chalgye) was the second son of the king. He ascended the throne in Gengwu and reigned for sixteen years. During this king's reign, the military forces of Baekje first began their incursions. This was the time of Emperor Min.
The fourth year of Jianxing, Guiyou (421 CE); the reign of Emperor Zhongzong of the Eastern Jin;
the fourth year of Daxing, Wuyin (367 CE), during the reign of Emperor Ming.

In the *yǒngchāng* (eternal prosperity) year of *rénwǔ*, the *dàníng* (great peace) year of *guīwèi*, the third year of King Hyeonjong’s reign (*xiǎnhóng*) in *bǐngxū*, and the ninth year of King Seongjong’s reign (*jiǎchǒu*), construction first began on the Bieok-bok (碧骨) embankment. It measured seventeen thousand twenty-six paces in circumference and one hundred sixty-six paces in width; the irrigated fields totaled fourteen hundred seventy-one *mu*. [Recorded by] the Tenth-generation King Won (原王).

The name is Jiao (釗). Furthermore, according to some accounts, it was established on the ridge [of Mount Gao] in the year Xinmao. Forty years later, in Jiawu, the walls of Pyeongyang were expanded. In the eighth month of Renyin, the capital was moved to Anseong (Ansi) City, which is the present-day Wando City.
In the second year of Jianyuan of Emperor Kang (the year Yiwei), and the second year of the twelfth cycle, the year Guimao, the twelfth King [ascended].
In the second year of Yul-ri (the *jiachen* year), during the reign of King Wonji of Fenxi, the twelfth son of King Na-mul-ma, who was the seventeenth king, was established.

His father was King Ku-do-geom-won (also known as King Mi-chao), his younger brother was King Mi-chu-gok-dan, and his mother was Lady Hu-rye of the Jin clan. In the fourth year of Yul-ri (the *bingchen* year), he ascended the throne. He reigned for forty-six years. His tomb is located to the southwest of Chansung Terrace. This was King Jin-so-gu, the thirteenth king.
The second son of Bi Liu, Bingwu, ascended the throne and reigned for twenty-nine years.
The fifth king, King Yipin, whose father was Juchi-mi and mother was Aji, ascended the throne on the Bingwu day and reigned for sixty years.
During the Shengping era, in the Ding-si year, he was the fifth Emperor Ai.
Lónghué (Renxū),
Xìngníng (Guǐhài), the three deposed emperors,
Dàhé (Bǐngyīn), and the fifth, Emperor Jiǎnwén.
Hyeon-an Sin-mi (17th year): The seventeenth, King So-gu (Soryeol), reigned for thirteen years; in Sin-mi, the capital was moved to Bupusan.
Yeongjong Ning-kang Gui-you (3rd year): The fourteenth, King Jin-ju.
He was the son of King Sinoggu. He ascended the throne in the year Yihae (1275) and reigned for nine years.
In the year Bŏngja of the Great Yuan (1336), he was twenty-one.
The eighteenth king was named Isuk, whose kingdom’s territory was at Jiji; he ascended the throne in the year Gapsin (1344) and reigned for eight years. The fifteenth king was Chinryu.

The nineteenth, King Gwanggae (Gwanggaeto), named Dammadeok, ascended the throne in the twenty-first year of the reign of King Jinchu (Jinjucheon) in the second year of Liri (551 CE); he ruled for twenty-one years until the twenty-ninth year of Emperor An’s Long’an era, the *dingyou* year (497 CE). The sixteenth, King Chinsu (Chinseong), ascended the throne in the *jia-shen* year (504 CE).

The twentieth, King Chesi (Cheonseong), ascended the throne in the *renchen* year (532 CE). He ruled for twenty-one years. The nineteenth was King Gwanggae, named Dammadeok; he ascended the throne in the *renchen* year (532 CE) and ruled for twenty-one years. The sixteenth was King Chesi.
Chinryū (枕流), younger brother of the King, ascended the throne in the year *Biyǒu* (乙酉) and reigned for seven years.
The seventeenth was Asin (阿莘, also written as Kaho-hōshin 河芳辰), his son; he ascended the throne in *Jinchen* (壬辰) and reigned for thirteen years.
In the first year of Yuánxīng, *Jinyǐn* (壬寅), the eighteenth, Shishengmālìgān (實聖麻立干) ascended the throne.

One source calls him King Sijju; another, King Po-gum. His father was King Mimi-ju, his younger brother was King Tae-seo-jik-kok-gan, his mother was Lady Ye-sin, and his consort was Lady A-ryu. He ascended the throne in the year *Ren-yin* and reigned for fifteen years. This king was the father of King Chi-seok.
He was the eighteenth king, King Jin-ji (also written as King Jin-ji), whose name was Eong-a-seon. He ascended the throne in the year *Yeoh-si* and reigned for fifteen years.
In the *Yixi* year *Yeoh-si*, he was the fourteenth [ruler]. The nineteenth was King Nol-gi-ma-ril-gan.

One version states: [King] Naemul’s father was King Jinjiwang and his mother was Lady Naemulhi of the Kim clan, daughter of King Mijuwang. He ascended the throne in the year Ding-si and reigned for forty-one years.
His son, King Changsu (the twentieth ruler), whose personal name was Sin-yeon, ascended the throne in Gui-chu and reigned for seventy-nine years.

His sixth successor, King Joo (also known as King Geumto), whose father was King Ipim and mother was Lady Jeongsin, ascended the throne in Ding-wu and reigned for fourteen years. [He was succeeded by] King Gong.
Yuanxi Jiwu (459–460 CE), the first year of Yongchu of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty (470 CE);
nineteen years later, in the seventh year of King Tienji’s reign, his son Gengshen ascended the throne and ruled for seven years; this was the seventh cycle of the *chuīxī* era.
One account states that King Geumhui’s father sat upon the throne; knowing his mother’s fortune, he established the governance in the *Xinyou* year and reigned for thirty years.

During the *Jingping* era of Emperor Xiaowu, in the *Guihai* year, and the *Jiazi* year of Emperor Wen’s *Yuanjia* era—specifically the *Dingmao* year—he moved the capital to the city of Pyeongyang. This was the reign of King Sejo.
The Great Prime, Gengyi (the first year of the sexagenary cycle), the twentieth [regnal year];
after King Biryu had ruled for a long time, King Sinji ascended the throne on Dingmao in the eighth year, and he governed for twenty-eight years.
The eighth, King Jichi—also known as King Geumjichi—ascended the throne on Sinmao in the thirty-sixth year of the reign of Queen Heomu Indeok.
In the *xiǎojian* (Xiàojiàn) era, year Jiǎwǔ (464), the third; in the *dà míng* (Dàmíng) era, year Dīngyōu (477), the eighth.

The twentieth: Cíbēi Mālìgān, of the Jīn clan; father Nùqí, mother Ālǎofū (one source reads Cìlǎofū), who was the daughter of a true sage-king. In the *wùxū* (Wùxū) era, she established [the reign] for twenty-one years. The twenty-first: Consort Bāhùgě Wénwáng’s daughter (one source reads □chì xījiǎogān, another reads □□jiǎogān), daughter of Gài lǔwáng.
One account states that the King of Koguryo, named Kyōngsi, was established in power in the year Yi-mi (475) and ruled for twenty years.

During the eighth year of Taishō of Emperor Daizong (513), specifically the year Yi-sa (525), and the fourth year of Yuánhuí of the deposed Emperor (529), specifically the year Gui-chou (533), relations were first established with the kingdom of Wu (Japan). In the year Ji-wèi (539), the military forces of the Wa state came to invade; they began by constructing Minghuó City, entered it for refuge, and subsequently surrounded Liángzhōu City, but returned without success. This occurred during the reign of Emperor Shùn.
In the second year of Shengming, the Ding-si year (477), King Wenzhou—also known as King Wenzhang—ascended the throne;
he was the son of King Galeu. In the Yi-mao year (479), he established the capital at Xiongchuan and reigned for two years.
In the third year, King Sanjin ascended the throne.
One version states he was the son of King Wangju. He ascended the throne in the second year of Liri (Jia-wei), the fourth year of the Jianyuan era of Emperor Taizu of Qi.
Twenty-first: Pichuma. One version states he was the son of King Jinji, the third son of King Jibim.

His mother was the daughter of Mungi-gokgan. He ascended the throne in the twenty-first year [of his reign], the Jia-wei year. His consort was the daughter of King Gibo-geumwang. Twenty-fourth: Dongseongwang.

The name is Moudai (alternatively transcribed as Madai), also known as Yuda (alternatively transcribed as Gaoyun). He was the younger brother of King Zhijin. He ascended the throne on the day of Jiwu and reigned for twenty-six years.
During the tenth year of Emperor Wu’s Yongming era, the year Guihai, he was deposed for the eleventh time. The twenty-first [successor] was King Wenzi, whose personal name was Mingli.
He was fond of the character "Yue" (Moon) and also styled Gaoyun. On the day of Renshen, he ascended the throne and reigned for twenty-seven years. The ninth [son] was King Qianzhi.
His father was Chich; he knew his maternal grandfather, Bangwon. In the year Ren-shen, he ascended the throne and reigned for twenty-nine years.
During the Jian-hu era of Gaozong, it was Ji-xu; in the fourth year, Yongtai, it was Wu-yin.
Yongyuan Jīmǎo (2nd year), the 22nd [reign year], Zhì Dìng Málìgān (also written as Zhìzhé;

his name was also Zhìdùlù). Of the Wang clan. Father: King Nùqí. Brother: King Qībǎogéwén. Mother: Lady Wūshēng, the daughter of King Nùqí. Consort: Lady Yíngdìfú, née Jiànlǎndài Hànzhī, a daughter of Duke Jué. Gēngchén, the 14th year of Lìlǐ, the Zhōngxīng era of Emperor Hé.
Xīn sì. The above constitutes the Ancient Period.
The following section concerns the twenty-fifth king of the Middle Period, King Huneung (虎寧王), named Soma, who was the second son of the ruler of the Eastern City.

He ascended the throne on the day of Xin-si and reigned for twenty-two years. The *Nanshi* (History of the Southern Dynasties) states his name was Paru-rong (扶餘隆), which is an error; Rong was actually the crown prince of King Bojang (寶藏王). This is detailed in the *Tangshu* (Book of Tang).
[This entry follows] the eighteenth year of the Ren-wu cycle during the Tianjian era of Emperor Gaozu of Liang, and precedes the twenty-third king, King Beopheung (法興王).

The *Cefu Yuangui* (Imperial Encyclopedia) states that his courtesy name was Wonjong, his clan name was Geum, and his given name was Jin. His father was Jijeong, and his mother was Lady Yeongdi. The posthumous title of "Fa" (Dharma) began with him. He ascended the throne in the year *Gyap-mu* (574) and reigned for twenty-six years. His tomb is located to the north of Aegungsa Temple. His consort was Lady Bachi; she entered the monastic order under the name Fallyu and resided at Yongheungsa Temple. She was the first to implement the monastic precepts and the first to practice the Ten Major Precepts (*daśa-śīla*). She established the prohibition against killing on the days of the ten fasts (*daśa-parvan*) and ordained others as monks and nuns.
The twenty-second king was King Anjang, named Heungan. He ascended the throne in the year *Hap-hae* (639) and reigned for twelve years.
The twenty-sixth king was King Myeongnong, the son of Huneung. He ascended the throne in the year *Gis-i* (693) and reigned for thirty-one years.
Ordinary year, *gengzi*, the seventh month, the tenth day, the *chou* branch;

Wang Qianzhi’s son and daughter were seized. In the *xinchou* year, the state was established. In the twelfth year, the fourth year of Dàtōng, the *renzi* year, the territory was surrendered and the kingdom was abolished. From the *rentin* year to the *renzi* year, a total of four hundred and ninety years elapsed before the kingdom was abolished.
In the second year of Dàtōng, the *dingwei* year, the second ruler of Liao (Liaodong), King An’uan, ascended the throne.
The era name was Bǎoyíng (Precious Welcome). In the fourteenth year of Lìlǐ, the Jīyǒu year of Dàtōng (569), six [new eras] were established;
in the Bǐngchén year of Jiànyuán (596), this year, the practice of establishing official era names began for the first time.
The twenty-fourth king, King Jinheung (r. 632–647), whose name was Sinmaek (also written as Sinmang) and who belonged to the Jin clan;

his father was the younger brother of King Beopheung. He ascended the throne in the second year of the Yimao cycle of the Datong era (635). His mother was Lady Jijyo (also known as Lady Sikdo), of the Park clan. His consort was Lady Chungyo, the daughter of General Yeongsilgok. He shaved his head and became a nun in the Gengshen year (660). He reigned for thirty-six years.

The twenty-fourth king, King Yangwon (also known as King Yanggang), whose name was Pyeongheung; he ascended the throne in the Bichu year (685) and reigned for fourteen years. In the Eumwu year (698), he moved the capital to Siche and styled his state "Southern Parhae."
Zhongda Tong (546), Bingyin;
Dading Dingmao (547); Emperor Daobao of the Northern Qi, Gengwu (560); Hou Jing.
The Great Beginning:
Xinwei, the year of the founding of the state (the 17th Xinwei);
the third year of Chengsheng, Renshen, under Emperor Sanjing.
In the year of Shaothai Yihai (535), the twenty-seventh king,
named Gaoyouming, ascended the throne; he ruled for forty-four years until Datong Bingzi (576),
the first year of Emperor Gaozu of the Chen dynasty.
The third year of the Tianjia era of Emperor Wen (Gengchen), the twenty-fifth year of the Yongding era (Dingchou).
[He was] the Prince of Pingyuan (also written as Pinggang), named Yangcheng. It is said that he moved it from Gao[...]. On the day Jimao, he established the principle; thirty-one years [had passed].
Tiankang Bingxu; Guangda Dinghai;

The Great Foundation (Daegeon): Jichu (14). The Great Salvation (Hongje): Incheon (12). Twenty-fifth: King Jinji (True Wisdom), styled Geumrin (Golden Wheel)—also written as Saryun;

surnamed Geum. Father: King Jinheung. Mother: Daughter of Lady Mugan—also written as Lady Se-dyo; wife of Lady Park, daughter of Gonggi Ri-u—also written as Lady Park, daughter of Yi-ri-u. Reigned for four years. His rule declined; he was succeeded by King Sunbeop.
The twenty-sixth [ruler], King Jinpyeong (真平王), was named Baekjeong (白淨).

His father’s name is lost; his mother was Lady Iljonggeok (立宗葛), daughter of King Manhu (萬呼)—also known as Lady Manning (萬寧)—and his wife was Lady Haengnyun (行倫). The Queen Mother (妃) was Lady Maya (摩耶), of the Geum (金) clan, whose personal name was Bokhep (福肹). The Empress (后妃) was Lady Seongman (僧滿), of the Sun (孫) clan. He ascended the throne on the day Jihai (己亥) of the Zhide (至德) era and died on the day Guimao (癸卯) of the fourth month.
Jianfu (524–528) Jiachen;
Zhengming (528–539) Dingwei; the three reigns of Emperor Wen of Sui (581–604) Gengxu—(11th year); the twenty-sixth [ruler], Infant Yang Wang.
One source says his name was Yuán; another says Dàyuán. He established the capital in Gēngxū and reigned for thirty-eight years. His twenty-eighth successor, King Huì, was named Jì;
another source calls him Xiànwáng. He was the son of Wēidé. He ascended the throne in Wǔwǔ and reigned until Xīnyǒu of the Rénshòu era.
The fourth [ruler] was Emperor Yáng.
The second year of Daye, Year of Yichou, Month Twelve, Number Twenty-nine:
The Dharma King named Xiaoshun; furthermore, the Prince Xuanhui was established as Emperor Gong in the Year of Jiwu.
The third year of Yining, Year of Dingchou, Number Thirty: Emperor Wu.
Some say his courtesy name was Wǔkāng Xiàn and his childhood name was Yīqí Shāidé; he ascended the throne in the Gēngshēn year and reigned for forty-one years.
In the fifth month of the Wǔdé era of Emperor Taizǔ of the Táng dynasty (the twenty-seventh year), he was posthumously titled Róngliú Wáng.
His name was also Jiàchéng; he ascended the throne in the Wǔdé era and reigned for twenty-four years as Emperor Taizǒng.

In the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era, the year Dinghai (647 AD), Queen Sunde (Queen Seondeok) ascended the throne. Her name was De-man; her father was King Jinpyeong, and her mother was Lady Maya of the Geum clan.

She was the daughter of King Sin-gok. Having no male heir, the Queen established herself as ruler. She married King Geungwon. In the year Renchen (692 AD), she ascended the throne and ruled for sixteen years. In the year Jiamu (714 AD) of the Renping era, [King Munmu] ascended the throne and ruled for fourteen years. In the year Rennyin (702 AD), King Bojang ascended the throne and ruled for twenty-seven years. In the year Jiayou (756 AD), King Yiji ascended the throne. [Third] Eleventh: King Yiji. He ascended the throne in the year Jiayou (756 AD). He ruled for twenty-seven years. *Note:

Prince Mu ascended the throne in the *xinchou* year and reigned for twenty years.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gaozong’s Yonghui era, the *gengxu* year, the twenty-eighth Queen Jeondeok, whose name was Seongman, succeeded him.

She was of the Geum clan; her father was Jinpyeongwang, the younger brother of the king, and her mother was Lady Ani of the Park clan. Her slave was the daughter of Geumwang. Some say she was Yemyeong, but this is incorrect. She ascended the throne in the *dingwei* year and reigned for seven years. In the sixth year of the *wushen* year of the Dae-ho era, the above [are the remains] of the Sanguk (Middle-Age Holy Bones); the below [are the remains] of the Jinguk (Upper-Age True Bones).
The twenty-ninth [ruler], King Taejong Muyeol (reign name: Ch'unggu), was of the Kim clan and the son of Prince Chinji and Lady Lungch'un.

He was the son of King Chokmun of Geokbon. Lungch'un is also written as Lungsu. His mother was Lady Cheongmyeong, posthumously titled Queen Munjeong; she was the daughter of King Jinpyeong. The Consort was Lady Hundy, posthumously titled Queen Munmyeong; she was the younger sister of Yu Il and was known by the childhood name Munhe. He ascended the throne in Gya-yeom (705) and reigned for seven years.

The reign ended in Byeon-gyeong (762). In Byeong-chin (776), the state was abolished. From the auspicious beginning in Gim-mo (192 BCE) to Byeong-shin (776 CE), six hundred and seventy-eight years passed.
In the *Xinyou* year of the Longshuo era (661) and the *Jiazi* year of the third *Lingde* cycle (704), the thirtieth King of Goguryeo, Munmu, whose name was Pamin, ascended the throne.

He was the son of King Taejong; his mother was Lady Hundi, and his consort was Queen Jiaui (also written as Neuwanghuo). She was the daughter of Sanguk Haeyu. He reigned for twenty years from the *Xinyou* year. His tomb is located in Geon-eun, in Donghae.
Qianfeng Bingyin (598), two reigns;
Zongzhang Wuchen (668), two reigns; [the state] was abolished in Wuchen.
From Dongming Jia Shen (1044 BCE) to Wuchen (668 CE), a total of seven hundred and five years.
The first was in the gengwu year of the Xianheng era;

Tiaolu Jǐmǎo (659),

The Lady Kim’s name was Jeong-myeong, her courtesy name was Il-jo. Her father was Mun-ho, and her mother was Queen Jin-muk, the daughter of Lord Kim Un. She was enthroned in Sin-sa (1071), the eleventh year of King Yeoljong’s reign; she passed away in Im-chun (1082), the second year of King Hyeonjong’s reign, on the day of Gui-we.
Her posthumous title was Queen Hong-do. In Gwi-mi (1083), the third year of King Hyeonjong’s reign... [the text continues].
The Ming dynasty began in the year Jiashen;
the Chui-gong era was in the year Yiyou; the four-year Yongchang era was in the year Jichou of the Zhou dynasty.
Tian-shou (Gengyin), two reigns;
Chang-shou (Renchen), two reigns. The thirty-second king was King Xiaozhao (Li Gong)—also written as Hong—of the Jin clan.
His father was King Shenwen; his mother was Queen Shimu. He ascended the throne in Renchen. He reigned for ten years. His tomb is located east of Wangde Temple.
Yanchai (Jiawu), Tianche (Yiwei),
and Tongtian (Bingshen).
The Shen-gong era, Ding-you;
the Sheng-li era, Wu-xu;
and the second Jiu-shi era, Geng-zi.
Cháng'ān, Xīnchū (4th year), No. 33: King Shèngdé, named Xīngguāng, whose original name was Lóngjī, was the younger brother of Emperor Xiàozhāo.

His former consort was Queen Péizhāo, posthumously titled Yánzhēn; she was the daughter of Yuándà Āgàn. His latter consort was Queen Zhānwù, posthumously titled Zhàodé; she was the daughter of Shùnyuán Jiǎogàn. He ascended the throne in Rényīn and reigned for thirty-five years. His tomb is located one *lǐ* south of Dōngcūn; another account says it is within Yángchánggǔ. It belongs to the second emperor, Zhōngzōng, and dates to the Yīsì year of Shénlóng. Jinglong Dingwei (the third year), Zhongzong;
Jingyun Gengxu (the second year), Xuanzong;
Xuantian Renzi (the first year).
In the *kaeywon* (Kaiyuan) era, the *gichu* (guichou) year, the twenty-ninth [year], the thirty-fourth King Seongjeong (King Hyegyeong), surnamed Kim, whose personal name was Seonggyeong:

his father was King Seongdeok; his mother was Queen Sojade; his consort was Queen Hwemyeong, daughter of Prince Jinjong Gokgan. He ascended the throne in the *dingchou* year, the fifth year of his reign. At *Baryu-sa*, his remains were cremated and the ashes scattered in the East Sea.
In the *tambō* (Tianbao) era, the *nimu* (renwu) year, the fourteenth [year], the thirty-fifth King Geumjeong (King Deokmun).

The Lady Kim’s name was Hyeon-yeong. Her father was Seongdeok, and her mother was Queen Dowager Jojade. She was the daughter of Sammo-buin, who had no offspring after leaving the palace. She was the consort of the Queen Dowager Manwol. Her posthumous title was Gyeongchui Wanghu (Queen Dowager Gyeongchui; "Chui" is also read as "Muk"). She was the daughter of Ujung Gangan. She was enthroned in the 23rd year of King Yeol of the Later Three Kingdoms period (945). Her initial burial was at the western peak of Gyeongji-sa, where a tomb was constructed using refined stone. Later, she was reinterred at Yangchanggok. This occurred during the second year of Ganyeon (768) of Emperor Suseong’s reign, in the Bingshen year of Jide (1076). The second year of Shangyuan, gengzi;
the second year of Erbaoying, renyin; the Guangde era of Emperor Daizong, guiyou. The second year.
In the year Yi-si of Yongtai, the thirty-sixth ruler, King Hwigong (r.

763–776), of the Jin clan, named Gyeon-un, was enthroned. His father was Geondeok; his mother was Queen Manwol, formerly Lady Sinba, daughter of Ujeonggokgan; and his consort was Lady Changchang, daughter of Jinganggokgan. He reigned for fifteen years until the year Bim-mu of Daeryeok (796).
[The following entry concerns] the fourteenth year of King Dejong.
In the thirty-seventh year of the Jianzhong era, the *gengshen* year (780), King Wang Ji, named Liangxiang, posthumously honored as King Kaesung, was born.

He was the son of Prince Hyeongbang Haegan and the daughter of King Seongdeok, Lady Sujyo, posthumously titled Queen Jeongi. His consort was Queen Guju, the daughter of Prince Wangpim Hageon. He ascended the throne in the *gengshen* year and reigned for five years until the *jiazi* year of Xingyuan (784).
Jingyuan (貞元) Year Yichou (乙丑), the 38th year of the reign of King Wonsaeng (元聖王), surnamed Kim (金), named Gyeongsin (敬愼)—also written as Gyeongsin (敬信).

The *New History of the Tang* (*Tangshu*) states that his father was Hyoryang (孝讓), posthumously titled Daagan (大阿干) and later enfeoffed as King Myeongdeok (明德大王); his mother was Inmyeong (仁暎)—one source says she was Lady Jibung (知鳥夫人)—posthumously titled Queen Sojung (昭文王后); his consort was Lady Changgeun (昌近伊己), posthumously titled Lady Sujeong (淑貞夫人); his principal consort was Lady Sinseok (神述角干). He ascended the throne in the Year Yichou, the 14th year of his reign. His tomb is located at Gukseon (鵠寺), which is now part of Chongboksa (崇福寺). An inscription stone erected by his descendants exists there.
[Reign of] King Sojong (昭聖王), Year Yongjeong (永貞), Year Yibyu (乙酉), the 39th year of his reign.

One source states that King Jaseong (also known as Wang Jin) was named Jun’ung; his father was Prince Hyejong, and his mother was Queen Seongmuk, Princess of the House of Kuei-hua. He ascended the throne in the year Jīmǎo and passed away. [He was] the fortieth ruler, King Aejang (Wang Jin), named Chonghe (alternatively called Cheongmyeong);

his father was King Josung, and his mother was Queen Kuei-hua. He ascended the throne in the year Xīn-mǎo and reigned for ten years. On the nineteenth day of the seventh month of the fourth year of the Yuánhé era (Jǐchōu), he was assassinated by his two uncles, King Hyeondeok and King Heungdeok, both titled Ikan, and passed away. [This was during the reign of] King Heonjong.
The fourteenth year of the Yuanhe era, the Bingxu year (826), the forty-first [reign], King Hyeon-deok of the Jin clan, named Yonsung, the younger brother of Queen So-seong;

his consort was Gwi-seungnyang, posthumously titled Wangho, the daughter of Chonggong Gokgan. He ascended the throne in the Jichu year (809) and reigned for nineteen years. His tomb is located north of Chonrin Village. The fourth [reign] was that of King Munjong during the Changgyeong era, the Sinchul year (831).
The fifth was King Jeongjong.
In the second year of the Barye (Baoli) era, the forty-second king, King Heungdeok (興德王), of the Kim clan, named Gyeonghui (景暉), was born;

he was the younger brother of King Heondeok (憲德王) and the husband of Lady Changhwa (昌花夫人). His posthumous title was Queen Jeongmuk (定穆王后). She was the daughter of King Josaeng (昭聖王). She was enthroned in the Bingwu year, and during her reign of ten years, her tomb was located in the northern part of An-gang (安康), where she was buried together with Lady Changhwa on the Byeoho (比火) soil. This was in the ninth year of the Daeho (太和) era of King Munjong (文宗), the Dingwei year.

The forty-third [ruler], King Hyeokkon (reigned 836–839), whose personal name was Gaerong (also written as Tae-ung) of the Kim clan, was the son of Anggan Hyeonjeong, posthumously titled King Heungseong (also written as □). His mother was Lady Mido (also written as Sinnae or Baril), posthumously titled Queen Sundeung, who was the daughter of Daegan Chunghaeng. His consort was Queen Munmuk, the daughter of Daegan Chung-hyo (also written as Junggong). He ascended the throne in the *bingchen* year of the Kaicheng era (836);
his reign lasted two years. The forty-fourth [ruler] was King Min (also written as Min or Ai).

The Lady Kim, named Myeongbo, was the daughter of Junggong Gogdan (posthumously enfeoffed as King Seonang) and Lady Guba (posthumously enfeoffed as Queen Hwijeong). She was enfeoffed as Queen Sinui. Her consort was Lady Yeonggong, daughter of Yonggong Gogdan; she was established as queen on the day of Eumwu and passed away on the twenty-second day of the first month of Jihwi, at the age of forty-five.

The Lady Wang, named Yujung, was the daughter of Gunjeong Gogdan (posthumously enfeoffed as King Seongdeok) and Lady Jeonggo (posthumously enfeoffed as Queen Joo-rye In-hye Gang). She was enfeoffed as Queen Jeongchong.

One version states she was the daughter of the late Empress Myeonghae (明海). She ascended the throne in the fourth month of the year Jih-wei (己未) and passed away on the thirteenth day of the eleventh month.

[Reign] Forty-sixth. King Munseong (文聖), surnamed Kim (金), personal name Gyeong-eung (慶膺). Father: King Sinhu (神虎); Mother: Queen Jeongchong (貞從). [She succeeded] the late Empress and Queen Jomyeong (照明). She ascended the throne in the eleventh month of the year Jih-wei. She reigned for nineteen years. [Era Name: Hujong (虎宗).

the Dazhong era, the Ding-mao year (847), was the thirteenth. This is the forty-seventh [entry].

King Wanyin of Xian'an, whose name was Yi-jing, was the younger brother of Shenhuwang. His mother was Lady Xinming. He ascended the throne in the Wu-yin year and reigned for three years under Emperor Yizong.
In the fourteenth year of the Xian Tong era, the *gengchen* year, the forty-eighth king was King Jingwen (景文王), surnamed Wang, named Yinglian (膺廉).

His father was Qiming (啟明), a *juegan* (角干) who was posthumously enfeoffed as Yi (義)—also read Yi (懿)—Gong (恭) Great King; he was the son of King Xikang (僖康王). His mother was Lady Guanghua (光和夫人), daughter of Lord Shenhuwang (神虎王); his consort was Empress Wenzi (文資皇后), daughter of King Xian’an (憲安王). He ascended the throne in the *xin si* year and reigned for fourteen years.
In the sixth year of the Qianfu era of Emperor Xizong, the *jiawu* year, the forty-ninth king was King Xiankang (憲康王).

King Jin’s name was Jeong; his father was King Gyeongmun, and his mother was Queen Munja (alternatively said to be Queen Uimyeong). He ascended the throne in the year Yiwe (1215), eleven years after the establishment of the state.
He reigned for ten-one years until the year Gwangmyeong Gengzi (1240) and Zhonghe Xinchou (1241). He was the fifth king and ruled for fifty years. He was posthumously titled King Dingkang.
The Lady Kim’s name was Hyang-min; she was the younger sister of King Muae (Ming’ae). She ascended the throne on the day of Bingwu and passed away.
On the day of Yi-si in the year Guangqi (847), the fifty-first [ruler], Queen Sinseong (True Sage) Kim, whose name was Man-hyeon, succeeded her.

She was the biological younger sister of King Jeonggang (Dingkang). Her consort was the Duke of Goryeong, U Hyeong-dae. He was posthumously honored as King Hweseong. She reigned for ten years and abdicated the throne to her younger brother, King Hyogong, on the day of Ding-si. She passed away in the twelfth month and was cremated; her bones were scattered at the western side of Mount Mu-ryang (also written as Mi) in Hwangsan (Yellow Mountain), during the reign of Emperor Zhaozong.
Mendŭk (524–597): Wushen year;
Longji (605–616): Jiyou year;

In the Great Shun era, the year Gengxu (890), he first moved his capital to Beopnyun of Northwon; in the year Bingchen (916), to T’ŭkwon City—which is present-day Dongju; in the year Dingsi (917), he moved the capital to Songak-gun;
and in the second year of Jingfu, the year Renzi (952), King Hyeonwon first moved the capital to Gwangju.
The fifty-second [ruler], King Wang of Xiaogong (Wang Jishi), named Yao, son of King Huan Kang (Wang Xian) and Queen Wenzi (Wang Hou).
He ascended the throne in the Ding-si year and reigned for fifteen years. He was cremated at Beojeongsa Temple; his remains were interred on the eastern slope of Choji-dae Mountain.

The Lady Park’s name was Gyeong-hui (originally named Su-jong); her mother was Lady Jeong-hwa. Her maternal grandfather, General Sun-hong Gok-gan, was posthumously honored as King Seong-ho. Her maternal great-grandfather, General Won-rin Gok-gan, was the distant descendant of King A-da. Her father, General Mun-won I-gan, was posthumously enfeoffed as King Heung-yeom. Her maternal grandfather, General Woon-gwan Hae-gan, was posthumously enfeoffed as King Seon-seong. The Queen Consort was Lady Jasi (also known as Lady Eui-seong) of King Hyo-jasi. She ascended the throne in the fifth year of Il-ri (1390), following the cremation of her predecessor. Her remains were interred at Namganhyeon.
She reigned until the fourth month of the sixth year of Jeongmyeong (1458), for a total of fifty-four years, and was succeeded by King Gyeong-myeong.

The name of Mr. Park was Seong-yeong; his father was Sin-deok, and his mother was Queen Ja-seong. He was the son of Da-jun Gok-gan, who was posthumously enfeoffed as King Seong-heui. Da-jun himself was the son of Su-jong I-gan. In the seventh year of the reign of King Yeol (Ding-chou), he established the practice of cremation at Hoang-bok-sa Temple, scattering the bones in the provinces; subsequently, in the year Jia-xu, he returned to Cheorwon, where King Tae-jo resided.

In the sixth month of the *wùyǐn* year, Yi died; the Great Ancestor ascended the throne at the capital of Cheonjeon. In the *jǐmǎo* year, the capital was moved to Songak-gun. In this same year, he founded the monasteries of Seonwang-sa, Jachun-sa, Wangnyun-sa, Naediseok-sa, and Sana-sa; furthermore, he founded Cheonseon-yuan (also known as Puyeong-sa), Sinheung-sa, Munju-sa, and Tongji-sa—these ten great monasteries were all established in this year. In the *gēngchén* year, the Oil Market was established below Yuryam, which is why it is now colloquially called "Yurhae" (Market below Yuryam). In the tenth month, Daehyeong-sa was founded. Some say [the previous dates] refer to the *rénwǔ* year; others say it was founded in *rénwǔ*. Furthermore, Ilmyeok-sa was founded in *xīn sì* (some say *jiǎshēn*). Waediseok-sa, Shinjung-yuan, and Heungguk-sa were founded in *dìnghài*. Myo-sa was founded in *jǐchōu*. Guisan-sa was founded in *gēngyǐn*. Longde was installed in *xīnsì*. "This is surely a gift from Heaven to me, intended for my lineage," he thought,

naming him Jinwa (Golden Frog).

King Fulou passed away,
